title: Who Is Jesus?
subtitle: The seven “I am” sayings in John
description: In John’s Gospel, Jesus describes Himself seven times with the words “I am.” Each one is a window into who He is and what He offers. Spend a week getting to know Him.

lessons.title: The Bread of Life
explanation: The day before this conversation, Jesus fed a crowd of about five thousand men with five small loaves and two fish (John 6:1–14). Now the same crowd has tracked Him down across the Sea of Galilee. They are hungry again, and they want more.

Jesus gently exposes their motives: they came looking for Him not because they understood the sign, but because they ate their fill (verse 26). The bread had pointed to something greater, and they missed it. So He invites them to stop working for food that spoils and to seek the food that lasts.

The crowd remembers manna, the bread from heaven that fed Israel in the wilderness (Exodus 16). Jesus reminds them that it was God, not Moses, who gave that bread, and that the Father now gives the true bread from heaven, the One who comes down and gives life to the world.

Then comes the first of John’s seven “I am” sayings: “I am the bread of life” (verse 35). Bread was the most basic food of the ancient world, eaten every day and needed for survival. Jesus is saying that He is not an extra for spiritual people. He is what every human soul needs to truly live. Whoever comes to Him will not go hungry, and whoever believes in Him will never be thirsty.

Notice how welcoming the passage is. Jesus says that whoever comes to Him He will never drive away (verse 37). He came to do His Father’s will, and the Father’s will is that everyone who looks to the Son and believes in Him will have eternal life (verse 40). The bread is not earned. It is received.

We are often like that crowd. We come to Jesus for what He can do: fix a problem, ease a fear, give us a better day. He cares about all of that. But He offers more than a meal. He offers Himself, and in Him we find the satisfaction that nothing else can give.
questions: What “food that spoils” are you tempted to chase for satisfaction: success, approval, comfort, something else?
Jesus says He will never drive away anyone who comes to Him (verse 37). How does that promise change the way you approach Him today?
What would it look like for you to “come to Jesus” for daily strength the way you come to the table for daily bread?
lessons.application: Before each meal today, pause for a few seconds and thank Jesus that He is the Bread of Life. Let ordinary hunger remind you of your deeper need for Him.
lessons.prayer: Jesus, You are the Bread of Life. Forgive me for looking to other things to fill me. Thank You that You never turn away anyone who comes to You. Today I come to You. Satisfy my soul. Amen.

lessons.title: The Light of the World
explanation: Jesus spoke these words in Jerusalem, in the temple courts, during or just after the Feast of Tabernacles (John 7:2, 37). This joyful festival remembered how God guided and cared for Israel in the wilderness, where He led them by a pillar of cloud by day and a pillar of fire by night (Exodus 13:21). Jewish tradition describes great lamps being lit in the temple courts during the feast, filling the city with light.

Into that setting Jesus announces, “I am the light of the world” (verse 12). It is a bold claim. Light in Scripture is closely tied to God Himself: “The LORD is my light and my salvation” (Psalm 27:1). The prophets promised that God’s light would shine on people living in darkness (Isaiah 9:2). Jesus is saying that this promised light has arrived, and it is Him.

Notice that He is the light of the world, not only of Israel. His light is for every nation, every neighborhood and every heart. And notice the promise attached: whoever follows Him will never walk in darkness but will have the light of life.

Light does at least three things. It reveals what is really there, both beauty and dirt. It guides, so we can see the path ahead. And it gives life, since nothing grows without it. Jesus does all three. He shows us the truth about ourselves and about God, He guides our steps, and He gives us life.

The Pharisees immediately push back, questioning whether His testimony is valid (verse 13). Jesus answers that He knows where He came from and where He is going, and that the Father who sent Him testifies with Him. Their problem was not a lack of evidence. They did not know the Father, so they did not recognize the Son (verse 19).

Following the light does not mean we will never face hard or confusing seasons. It means we never walk through them alone or without direction. The One who is the light walks with us and goes ahead of us.
questions: Where in your life right now do you feel most “in the dark”: uncertain, confused, or afraid?
Light reveals what is hidden. Is there anything you have been keeping in the dark that you need to bring to Jesus?
What is one way you can follow Jesus’ light more closely this week?
lessons.application: Each time you turn on a light today, whisper a short prayer: “Jesus, You are my light. Lead me.” Bring one specific decision or worry into His light.
lessons.prayer: Lord Jesus, You are the light of the world. Shine into every corner of my heart. Show me what is true, guide my next steps, and fill me with Your life. I choose to follow You. Amen.

lessons.title: The Gate
explanation: Jesus uses a picture His listeners knew well: a sheepfold. In the countryside of that time, a sheepfold was often a simple stone enclosure with a single opening. At night the sheep were brought inside for protection, and the shepherd could lie down across the opening himself. He became the gate. Nothing could get in or out without going through him.

Jesus says, “I am the gate” (verses 7 and 9). This is the third “I am” saying in John. It speaks of access and safety. A gate is the way in. Through Jesus we enter into God’s family, God’s presence and God’s care. Whoever enters through Him will be saved, and will come in and go out and find pasture (verse 9).

That picture of coming in and going out is beautiful. It describes a life of security and freedom at the same time. Inside the fold there is rest and protection. Outside there is good pasture. Jesus does not confine His sheep. He leads them into a full, nourishing life.

Jesus contrasts Himself with thieves and robbers who climb in another way (verse 1). In the context of John 9, these are religious leaders who had just thrown out a man Jesus healed of blindness. Instead of caring for the sheep, they used and harmed them. Jesus came for the opposite reason.

Verse 10 sums up the difference: the thief comes only to steal, kill and destroy, but Jesus came that His sheep may have life, and have it to the full. Jesus is not a gatekeeper who keeps joy out. He is the gate that opens into life as God intended it.
In a world full of voices that promise life but leave us empty, Jesus invites us to come through Him and find safety, belonging and true abundance.
questions: What voices or influences in your life promise “life” but end up stealing your peace or joy?
Jesus offers both safety (coming in) and freedom (going out to pasture). Which of those do you need most right now, and why?
How would you describe “life to the full” in your own words?
lessons.application: Notice the doors you walk through today. At each one, thank Jesus that He is the Gate who welcomes you in, keeps you safe, and leads you to good things.
lessons.prayer: Jesus, You are the Gate. Thank You that through You I have been welcomed into God’s family. Protect me from anything that would steal, kill or destroy. Lead me into the full life You came to give. Amen.

lessons.title: The Good Shepherd
explanation: Right after calling Himself the gate, Jesus gives a fourth “I am” saying: “I am the good shepherd” (verse 11). For Jesus’ Jewish listeners, this picture would bring to mind Psalm 23, “The LORD is my shepherd,” and the promise in Ezekiel 34 that God Himself would come to search for His scattered sheep and care for them.

Shepherding was hard, humble work. A shepherd led his flock to food and water, guarded them from wild animals and thieves, carried the weak, and searched for the lost. Jesus says He is the good shepherd: not merely competent, but noble, beautiful and trustworthy.

What makes Him good? Above all, the good shepherd lays down His life for the sheep (verse 11). A hired hand runs when the wolf comes, because the sheep are not really his (verses 12–13). Jesus will not run. He will give everything, even His life, for those He loves. He does this freely: no one takes His life from Him; He lays it down of His own accord, and He has authority to take it up again (verse 18). Jesus is pointing ahead to the cross and the empty tomb.

The good shepherd also knows His sheep personally (verse 14). Not as a crowd, but one by one. He knows your name, your story and your struggles, and He knows them with the same closeness that the Father and the Son share (verse 15).

Finally, Jesus mentions other sheep that are not of this fold (verse 16). He came for people of every nation and background, gathering them into one flock under one Shepherd. No one is outside the reach of His care.
We can be anxious, wandering and easily distracted, much like sheep. The good news is not that we are strong, but that our Shepherd is good.
questions: Which part of the good shepherd’s care (leading, protecting, knowing, searching, sacrificing) means the most to you today?
How does knowing that Jesus laid down His life willingly for you affect the way you see yourself?
Is there an area of your life where you’ve been acting like your own shepherd? What would it look like to let Jesus lead?
lessons.application: Read Psalm 23 slowly today, maybe out loud. Each time it says “the LORD,” remember that Jesus is the Good Shepherd who gave His life for you.
lessons.prayer: Good Shepherd, thank You for knowing me by name and for laying down Your life for me. When I wander, bring me back. When I am afraid, stay close. Lead me today, and help me follow Your voice. Amen.

lessons.title: The Resurrection and the Life
explanation: Lazarus and his sisters, Martha and Mary, were close friends of Jesus. When Lazarus fell seriously ill, the sisters sent word to Jesus. Surprisingly, He waited two more days before going (John 11:6). By the time He arrived in Bethany, Lazarus had been in the tomb four days.

Martha meets Jesus on the road with honest grief: “Lord, if You had been here, my brother would not have died” (verse 21). Jesus doesn’t scold her. He speaks the fifth “I am” saying: “I am the resurrection and the life” (verse 25). Whoever believes in Him will live, even though they die. Then He asks her a personal question: “Do you believe this?” Martha answers with one of the clearest confessions of faith in the Gospels (verse 27).

When Mary comes and falls at His feet, saying the same words as her sister, Jesus responds differently. He is deeply moved and troubled, and He weeps (verses 33–35). This is one of the most tender moments in Scripture. Jesus knew He was about to raise Lazarus, and still He wept with His friends. He does not hurry us past our pain. He enters it with us.

Then He stands at the tomb, prays to the Father, and calls in a loud voice, “Lazarus, come out!” (verse 43). The man who was dead walks out, still wrapped in grave clothes. Jesus is not only able to comfort us in death; He has authority over death itself.
This sign pointed forward to Jesus’ own resurrection just days later. Because He rose, everyone who trusts Him has a living hope. Death is real and grief is real, but neither has the final word.

Notice that Jesus’ delay was not a lack of love (verse 5 says He loved them). Sometimes His timing confuses us. This story invites us to trust both His heart and His power, even when we don’t understand His timing.
questions: Martha and Mary both said, “Lord, if You had been here…” Is there a disappointment you have brought to Jesus with the same honesty?
What does it mean to you that Jesus wept, even though He knew He would raise Lazarus?
Jesus asked Martha, “Do you believe this?” How would you answer Him today?
lessons.application: Think of someone who is grieving or discouraged. Reach out today with a short message, a call or a small act of kindness, and pray for them by name.
lessons.prayer: Jesus, You are the resurrection and the life. Thank You that You weep with me in sorrow and that You have power over death. Help me trust Your heart when I don’t understand Your timing. I believe; help my faith to grow. Amen.

lessons.title: The Way, the Truth and the Life
explanation: It is the night before the cross. Jesus is with His closest friends in the upper room. He has washed their feet, predicted His betrayal, and told Peter he will deny Him. Then He says He is going away. The disciples are confused and afraid.

Jesus begins with comfort: “Do not let your hearts be troubled” (verse 1). He invites them to trust God and to trust Him. He speaks of His Father’s house with many rooms, and promises that He is going to prepare a place for them, and that He will come back and take them to be with Him (verses 2–3). Heaven is described here most of all as being with Jesus.

Thomas, honest as ever, says what the others are thinking: “Lord, we do not know where You are going, so how can we know the way?” (verse 5). Jesus answers with the sixth “I am” saying: “I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through Me” (verse 6).

Jesus doesn’t hand Thomas a map. He offers Himself. He is the way, so we come to God through Him. He is the truth, so in Him we see what God is really like. He is the life, so in Him we receive the life of God. Then He adds that whoever knows Him knows the Father (verse 7).

These words are both exclusive and wide open. Jesus claims to be the one way to the Father, and that way is open to anyone who comes to Him: Thomas with his questions, Peter with his failures, and you and me.

When life feels uncertain and the road ahead is unclear, Jesus doesn’t ask us to figure everything out first. He asks us to trust Him and walk with Him. He is the way, even when we can’t see the whole path.
questions: What is troubling your heart right now? Write it down and hand it to Jesus.
Thomas asked an honest question and Jesus welcomed it. What question would you like to bring to Jesus?
Which of the three (Way, Truth or Life) do you most need Jesus to be for you this week?
lessons.application: Memorize John 14:6 today. You can add it to My Verses in the Grow tab. When you feel uncertain, repeat it as a reminder that Jesus Himself is your way forward.
lessons.prayer: Jesus, You are the way, the truth and the life. When my heart is troubled, help me trust You. Thank You for preparing a place for me and for the promise that I will be with You. Lead me to the Father, one step at a time. Amen.

lessons.title: The True Vine
explanation: Jesus gives His seventh and final “I am” saying in John, still on the night before the cross: “I am the true vine, and My Father is the keeper of the vineyard” (verse 1). In the Old Testament, Israel was often pictured as a vine that God planted and tended (Psalm 80:8; Isaiah 5:1–7). Jesus calls Himself the true vine. In Him, God’s people find their life and their fruitfulness.

The picture is simple. Branches don’t produce fruit by straining harder. They bear fruit by staying connected to the vine, where the life flows from. Jesus says, “Apart from Me you can do nothing” (verse 5). Our job is not to manufacture fruit but to remain, or abide, in Him.

What does it mean to abide? In this passage it includes letting His words remain in us (verse 7), praying (verse 7), keeping His commands (verse 10), and remaining in His love (verse 9). It is a daily relationship of listening, trusting, obeying and receiving love.

The Father, as the keeper of the vineyard, also prunes the branches that bear fruit so they will be even more fruitful (verse 2). Pruning can be uncomfortable. Sometimes God trims away things in our lives, even good things, to make room for better growth. Pruning is not punishment; it is the careful work of a vinedresser who wants His plants to flourish.

And what is the fruit? Throughout the New Testament, fruit includes a Christlike character (Galatians 5:22–23), love for others, and lives that point people to God. Jesus says that this glorifies the Father and shows that we are His disciples (verse 8).

Jesus ends with a beautiful purpose: He has said all this so that His joy may be in us and our joy may be complete (verse 11). Abiding in Jesus is not a heavy burden. It is the way to the deepest joy there is.
questions: Where are you trying to “bear fruit” by your own effort instead of staying connected to Jesus?
What helps you abide in Jesus day to day? What gets in the way?
Can you see any “pruning” God may be doing in your life? How might He be using it for growth?
lessons.application: Choose one simple daily habit for abiding this week, such as reading a chapter, praying for five minutes, or memorizing a verse, and put it on your calendar.
lessons.prayer: Jesus, You are the true vine and I am a branch. I can do nothing apart from You. Help me remain in Your love today. Prune what needs to go, and let Your life produce fruit in me, so that the Father is glorified and my joy is complete. Amen.
